meta.what: Round 13: remittances from Russia at the migrant's net gain. Wages pay for real work, so only the part above the migrant's alternative wage is a gain, and only the war-driven change above the no-war baseline counts.
meta.formula: counted (toward Russia) = L x w + p x extra x (L x (1 - w) - E). L = labour remittances, E = expected without the war (remittances.json); w = the war wage premium, the share of the Russian wage above its pre-war trend; p = the premium over the alternative wage, 1 - alternative / migrant wage in Russia without the war; extra = remittances.json's genuinely extra share (channel shift from cash to cards, other destinations)
meta.why: the war wage premium (L x w) is pay above what the same work earned before the war, a gain to the migrant's country; the rest of the change (more or fewer migrants, at no-war wages) is a gain only by the margin over what those workers earn elsewhere

TJK.note: The World Bank total (10.18) is 6% above what EFSD's 54.5% of GDP implies (9.62). The audit's 'about 8.6bn' is not in the article it cites (Times of Central Asia gives 45% of GDP for 2024 and an ADB forecast of 37% for 2025). The research keeps the World Bank total with its range; the low end of 2025 labour (4.6bn EUR) already covers EFSD's figure. The Bank of Russia publishes no country split since 2021.

UZB.note: Central Bank of Uzbekistan, brief review of individuals' currency operations, via Kun.uz and Times of Central Asia (20 Jan 2025): matches remittances.json. Uzbeks working abroad fell by a third in 2024 to 1.14m (about 1m in Russia), so the rise is pay per worker and channel shift, not more workers.
